newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Member states protest at delay "threat" to BSE beef moves.
newsitem.headline: Member states protest at delay "threat" to BSE beef moves.

text.p: European Union member states have protested at the threat of a long delay to proposals for the identification of animals and beef labelling, EU officials and diplomats said.

A Commission decision to change the legal base of the two proposals, which are aimed at restoring public confidence after the mad cow crisis, was decribed as "crazy" by some delegates at the special agricultural committee on Monday, a diplomat said.

The decision introduces the "co-decision procedure," involving lengthy discussions between the European Parliament, Council of Ministers and the Commission. It effectively gives the Parliament a right to veto legislation it does not like.

Last week the parliament raised the prospect of delays by calling for changes to last October's proposals (COM(96)460), demanding that beef labelling be compulsory from the outset and to do away with cattle passports if the data was stored on computers.

Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler informed the Dutch EU presidency this week that new proposals will be presented despite the fact that the two measures are close to being adopted as EU law, a presidency official said.
The issue is due to be discussed again by EU ambassadors meeting in COREPER on Wednesday when Denmark and Finland which reserved their position on Monday will announce their views.
"If the Commission is to present a new proposal changing the legal base to introduce co-decision with the European Parliament you have a situation that could last a year," a Dutch official said.

Last week European Commission President Jacques Santer told MEPs in a debate on the findings of the European Parliament committee of inquiry into BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) that all legislative decisions should in future be subject to co-decision and that he hoped this would also apply to the CAP (Common Agricultural Policy).

"He said that all veterinary and phyto-sanitary (plant health) legislation would be under article 100a but no one expected a sudden change in the legal base of the identification and beef labelling proposals which are close to a conclusion," one diplomat said.
Several delegations were said by diplomats present at Monday's committee meeting to have challenged the legality of the Commission's move.

They said that the Commission must conform with past European Court of Justice rulings that the co-decision procedure providing for majority voting in Council (Art 100 a) should apply to "general single market legislation".
"Legislation specifically relating to agriculture and the CAP should be under article 43 and it would require a decision in the Inter Governmental Conference to change that," said a British official.

Typically proposals dealt with under the co-decision procedure can take two years to implement although diplomats say one delegate at Monday's meeting had calculated that it was "theoretically" possible to conclude identification and labelling by April.
"This would assume that the Parliament accepts that the opinions it has already expressed under article 43 can be taken as part of the 100a process, a diplomat said.

The Dutch presidency says that uncertainty now surrounds a number of agricultural proposals. "We are continuing to chair discussions. We still have article 43 items but we do not know if the Commission will change it," a Dutch government official said.
